Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that continuously reads the voltage from a Honeywell MICROpeL MP-741 combustible gas sensor through an MCP3008 ADC on the SPI bus using CE0, channel 0, with a 1 MHz SPI clock, operates in single‑ended mode, retries any ADC read failure after a 100 ms delay, prints the measured voltage and a placeholder PPM value to the console once per second, and appends a timestamp, voltage, and PPM to a file named gas_log.txt while checking for SPI initialization errors, SPI transfer failures, and file open errors; the program must install a SIGINT handler so that pressing Ctrl +C triggers clean closure of the SPI interface and graceful termination of the driver library, ensuring proper resource cleanup on all exit paths, and it should run as a simulated propane leak detector until interrupted.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that reads the X, Y, and Z acceleration signals from an ADXL335 analog accelerometer using an MCP3008 10‑bit ADC on SPI mode 0, with the ADXL335 X‑out connected to MCP3008 channel 0, Y‑out to channel 1, and Z‑out to channel 2, the MCP3008 chip‑select tied to GPIO8 (BCM), MOSI to GPIO10 (BCM), MISO to GPIO9 (BCM), and SCLK to GPIO11 (BCM); the program must initialize the SPI bus and each channel, verify every initialization step and each SPI transaction, gracefully handle cases where the sensor is absent or the bus reports errors, apply a Kalman filter to the raw 10‑bit samples from each axis using the 3.3 V reference to produce smoothed acceleration values in g, print the filtered X, Y, and Z values to the console at a steady rate of 10 Hz, and ensure that all resources are cleanly released on every exit path, including proper handling of SIGINT and SIGTERM signals.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that reads three Texas Instruments DRV5055VA Hall‑Effect sensors as digital logic states on individual GPIO pins (sensor 1 on GPIO4 BCM, sensor 2 on GPIO17 BCM, sensor 3 on GPIO27 BCM) every 100 milliseconds, simulates an ADC by interpreting HIGH as 3.3 V and LOW as 0.0 V, converts each state to a magnetic field strength value, and logs the three computed values in millitesla to a file named magnetic_log.txt in a comma‑separated line format “sensor1_mT,sensor2_mT,sensor3_mT”, flushing the file after each write; the program must include robust error handling for GPIO access and file I/O, printing a warning to stderr whenever any computed magnetic field falls outside the range –100 mT to +100 mT, skipping the logging for that iteration if any GPIO read fails, using only individual API call() operations for broad compatibility, and must handle SIGINT (Ctrl‑C) to perform a graceful shutdown that releases all driver resources properly.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that continuously reads the soil moisture sensor through an MCP3008 ADC on the SPI bus (CE0, 500 kHz, mode 0) using channel 0 in single‑ended mode, evaluates the moisture level every 60 seconds, and drives a pump relay connected to GPIO17 (BCM, active‑high) so that the pump is turned on when the moisture reading falls below 30 % and turned off when it rises to 30 % or above, while logging every event—including program start, each pump on/off transition, any errors, and program termination with timestamps—to a file named “watering.log”, handling errors by checking all driver and SPI calls and logging any ADC read failures but continuing operation, and ensuring a clean shutdown by installing signal handlers for SIGINT and SIGTERM that turn the pump off before exiting.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that continuously reads analog values from three single‑ended MCP3008 channels (0, 1, and 2) over the SPI bus /dev/spidev0.0 (SPI0, CE0, SPI_MODE_0, 8 bits per word, 1 MHz) and logs the readings once per second to a CSV file named sensor_data.csv, with each line containing the three channel values in order; the program must check the result of every open, ioctl, read, and write call and, on any failure, print an error message and exit gracefully, and it must also install a SIGINT handler so that when the user presses Ctrl +C the CSV file is properly closed and the SPI resources are released before the program terminates.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that subscribes over MQTT on TCP to mqtt.eclipseprojects.io:1883, listening on the topic “home/led_control” with client ID “rpi_led_control” and QoS 0, parses each incoming JSON payload expecting exactly the key “led_state” with a boolean value, rejects any other keys or types, and drives an LED connected to GPIO17 (BCM) as output, turning the LED off at startup, setting the pin HIGH when led_state is true and LOW when false; the program must implement robust error handling that logs all connection failures, JSON parsing errors, and protocol violations to stderr with timestamps, and uses an exponential reconnection backoff starting at 1 s, then 2 s, 4 s, and so on up to a maximum of 60 s; it must employ the provided MQTT client callbacks with a start/stop loop, use the supplied JSON parsing utility, and control the GPIO via the given driver API calls, while installing signal handlers for SIGINT and SIGTERM to perform a clean shutdown that disconnects from MQTT, turns off the LED, and releases all driver resources, guaranteeing that every exit path—whether normal, error, or signal‑driven—leaves no resources allocated.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that continuously reads the digital output (DO) of a KY‑038 sound sensor module on a single‑bit GPIO bus, using the sensor’s DO pin connected to GPIO17 (BCM numbering), and prints the sound level reading (0 or 1) to the console each loop iteration with a 100 ms delay between reads; when the sensor reports a sound event—remembering that the KY‑038 DO pin goes LOW when the detected sound exceeds the onboard potentiometer threshold—the program must trigger an alarm LED attached to GPIO18 (BCM) by turning the LED on for 1 s and then off, and continue monitoring; the implementation must verify successful initialization of the GPIO driver, successful opening of the chip, successful line request, and must check the result of every I/O operation, handling sensor‑absent or bus‑error conditions gracefully by printing an error message and exiting; finally, the program must catch SIGINT (Ctrl‑C) or SIGTERM and cleanly release all GPIO lines before exiting, ensuring proper resource cleanup on all exit paths.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that monitors the SW‑420 vibration sensor connected to GPIO17 (BCM, physical pin 11) via the /dev/gpiochip0 GPIO character device, requesting the single line with the consumer label “vibration‑monitor” and configuring it for falling‑edge detection because the sensor’s DO output is active‑low, open‑collector (idle HIGH, pulls LOW when vibration exceeds the threshold). The program must robustly check every driver call (opening the chip, obtaining the line, requesting the event, waiting for an event, reading the event) and every file I/O call (opening /var/log/vibration_shutdown.log in append mode, writing with a timestamped line, and closing), reporting any failure with perror, and must install SIGINT and SIGTERM handlers that set a volatile sig_atomic_t flag so the main loop can exit cleanly; on each detected falling‑edge event the program should read the event using the single‑line event API, append a timestamped message to the log file and also print the same message to stdout, then invoke system("sudo shutdown -h now"); finally, on every exit path the code must release the GPIO line and close the chip to clean up all resources.

prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that reads an LM35 analog temperature sensor through an MCP3008 10‑bit ADC connected on SPI0 using chip‑enable CE0 and GPIO pins 8, 9, 10, 11, sampling the temperature every 5 seconds, storing each reading as a float in a circular buffer of 120 entries, printing each value to the console in the exact format “Temperature: XX.XX °C”, and after each sample overwriting the entire buffer to a binary file named temp_log.dat opened in mode wb+ so that the file always contains exactly 120 float values with the oldest data replaced when the buffer wraps; the program must verify successful initialization of the driver, opening of the SPI device, and each SPI transfer, printing an error and skipping the current reading if a transfer fails while continuing operation, and if the file cannot be opened it must print an error and continue without file logging; finally, it must install signal handlers for SIGINT and SIGTERM that close the SPI interface, terminate the driver cleanly, and exit gracefully.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that reads the ambient light from a BH1750 I2C light sensor on the I2C bus (/dev/i2c-1) and the sound level from a MAX4466 analog microphone connected to channel 0 of an MCP3008 ADC accessed via the SPI bus (/dev/spidev0.0), samples both sensors once per second, and appends each reading to a file named environmental_log.txt using the format “YYYY‑MM‑DD HH:MM:SS, Light: [lux], Sound: [raw ADC value]”, while handling any I2C or SPI communication errors and sensor‑absent conditions without crashing, and ensuring that all resources are cleanly released and the program terminates gracefully on receipt of SIGINT or SIGTERM, all without using any existing driver library.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that reads the digital output of a Keyes KY‑026 flame sensor module connected to the GPIO bus as a digital input on BCM pin 17, initializing the line for input with a pull‑down resistor, then polls the pin once every second, logging each reading to a CSV file named flame_events.log with columns timestamp, pin and state, and printing an alarm message to stdout whenever the sensor reports a HIGH (active HIGH on flame); the program must check the result of every driver library API call (the library’s API call*, the library’s API call*) and on any failure print an error message to stderr and exit with a non‑zero status, and it must clean up all GPIO resources both on normal termination and when receiving SIGINT or SIGTERM.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that continuously reads the TMP36 analog temperature sensor connected to channel 0 of an MCP3008 ADC using the SPI bus with chip‑enable CE0 at a 500 kHz clock, converts the raw ADC value to degrees Celsius, and then drives an MCP4725 DAC on the I2C bus to output a voltage proportional to the measured temperature; the program must sample every 0.5 seconds, log each reading to a file named temperature_log.txt with a timestamp, the raw ADC count, the calculated temperature in °C, and the DAC voltage, also echoing the same information to stdout, and must include robust error handling that checks all initializations, SPI transfers, I2C writes, and file operations, gracefully handling sensor‑absent or bus‑error conditions with retries and clear error messages, and must perform a clean shutdown on receipt of SIGINT by closing the SPI interface, the I2C interface, the log file, and terminating any driver resources, while adhering to the constraint of not using any driver library or deprecated APIs.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that reads moisture from three DFRobot Soil Moisture Sensor v2.0 analog resistive sensors connected to an MCP3008 ADC via the SPI bus on CE0, mode 0 at 1 MHz, with the sensors wired to MCP3008 channels 0, 1, and 2, then sleeps for 60 seconds between cycles, appends each reading to a file named soil_data.txt in the format “YYYY‑MM‑DD HH:MM:SS” with one line per sensor per cycle, prints an error and exits with code 1 if any of the required driver functions fail, prints an error and continues if an ADC value is invalid, and on receipt of SIGINT closes the SPI interface, closes the log file, terminates the driver, and prints a goodbye message, ensuring proper resource cleanup on all exit paths while using only the provided driver functions.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that sequentially activates and deactivates four Songle SRD-05VDC-SL relay modules connected as a light sequencer on the GPIO digital output bus, using BCM pins 17, 22, 23, and 24 for relays 1‑4 respectively; the program must initially set all relay pins to inactive (LOW, assuming active‑high relays), then in an infinite loop activate each relay for one second, deactivate it, wait one second before moving to the next relay, and repeat this pattern indefinitely, while checking the result of every driver library call (the library's API call, the library's API call, etc.) for errors, providing clear comments throughout, and installing a signal handler for SIGINT and SIGTERM that, on exit, deactivates all relays and releases all GPIO lines; no SPI, ADC, temperature sensor, or logging functionality may be used and only standard C libraries together with the driver library may be employed.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that continuously reads the analog output of a Keyes KY-038 sound sensor connected to channel 0 of an MCP3008 ADC over the SPI bus CE0 on GPIO 8 using mode 0 at 1 MHz, sampling every 10 ms, and when the measured value exceeds a defined threshold it must turn on an LED wired to GPIO 16 (BCM) for 500 ms, log the event with a timestamp in the format “YYYY‑MM‑DD HH:MM:SS” to a file named sound_events.log, apply a debounce delay after each trigger, and gracefully handle any SPI transfer failures, invalid ADC channel selections, or GPIO initialization errors by checking all driver library calls and file operations; the program must also install a SIGINT handler that on receipt cleanly releases resources by closing the SPI interface, terminating the driver library, and turning off the LED, and it must be written using the driver library, not the driver library.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that continuously reads the analog output of a Seeed Studio Grove Rain Sensor through an MCP3008 on SPI channel 0 configured at 1 MHz mode 0, polls the sensor once per second, appends the rain level together with a timestamp to a file named rain_log.txt (flushing after each write), and based on a default rain‑threshold value of 5 decides whether to close or open a window: when the measured level exceeds the threshold the program must drive a motor forward for exactly three seconds using the L298N‑based DC motor driver with IN1 connected to GPIO17 (BCM), IN2 to GPIO18 (BCM) and ENA (PWM) to GPIO27 (BCM) at a PWM duty of 150 within a range of 255, otherwise it must drive the motor in reverse for three seconds; the window is assumed initially open; the code must check every initialization, system call and I/O return value, handling failures to initialize the driver library, open the SPI device or the log file by printing clear error messages and performing proper cleanup, and must also detect and log any SPI transfer or file‑write errors without crashing; signal handlers for SIGINT and SIGTERM must set a volatile sig_atomic_t flag that causes the main loop to stop the motor, close the SPI interface, close the log file and terminate the driver library before exiting, and all resources must be released on any exit path; the program should be compiled with gcc -o rain rain.c -lthe driver library -lrt -lpthread.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi that opens the USB camera on /dev/video0 in blocking mode (O_RDWR without O_NONBLOCK), queries the device capabilities to ensure both V4L2_CAP_VIDEO_CAPTURE and V4L2_CAP_STREAMING are present, sets the pixel format to V4L2_PIX_FMT_MJPEG with a width of 192 (the documented value) and V4L2_FIELD_NONE, requests four MMAP buffers, starts streaming, dequeues a single frame, verifies that the dequeued buffer’s bytesused field is greater than zero, and writes the raw MJPEG bytes directly to a file named image.jpg without any re‑encoding; every ioctl, open, mmap, and fopen call must have its return value checked and any failure reported with a descriptive perror/errno message, and a SIGINT/SIGTERM handler must be installed to stop streaming, unmap all buffers, free the buffer array, close the file and the device file descriptor on all exit paths, ensuring clean resource release.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi that controls a camera pan‑tilt mount using the board’s GPIO software PWM bus and four active‑low push‑buttons with internal pull‑ups, where the pan servo is connected to GPIO4 (BCM) and the tilt servo to GPIO5 (BCM), the tilt‑up button to GPIO6 (BCM), the tilt‑down button to GPIO7 (BCM), the pan‑left button to GPIO8 (BCM) and the pan‑right button to GPIO9 (BCM); the program must generate a 50 Hz PWM period (20 ms) with pulse widths ranging from 1 ms to 2 ms (corresponding to duty values of 50 to 100 out of 1000), initialize both servos to the mid‑position value 75, and on each button press adjust the corresponding axis by ±5 while clamping the position to the range 25–125, poll the button states every 50 ms, check the return status of every driver call and handle any request failures, and on receipt of SIGINT cleanly release all allocated resources.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi running Bookworm 64‑bit that opens the USB camera on /dev/video0, uses select() with a 2‑second timeout to wait for a frame, requests buffers, memory‑maps them, queues a buffer, starts streaming, dequeues the captured frame, stops streaming, unmaps the buffers, frees them and closes the file descriptor, handling SIGINT so that all these steps are performed cleanly on interruption; the captured image, originally in the documented YUYV format, must be converted to RGB24, processed with a blur filter, then encoded as a JPEG file named capture_YYYYMMDD_HHMMSS.jpg with quality set to 75, and every system call and memory allocation must be checked for failure with error messages printed to stderr and all resources released before exiting.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi running a 32‑bit or 64‑bit kernel with the V4L2 subsystem active that opens the CSI camera device node /dev/video0, checks that the node exists and can be opened, queries the device capabilities with VIDIOC_QUERYCAP, enumerates all supported frame sizes using VIDIOC_ENUM_FRAMESIZES and for each size enumerates the available frame intervals with VIDIOC_ENUM_FRAMEINTERVALS, then queries the V4L2_CID_FOCUS_AUTO control with VIDIOC_QUERYCTRL to determine whether autofocus is supported, printing a clear, human‑readable summary of the resolutions, frame rates and autofocus capability to stdout; the program must verify every ioctl return value, handle the cases where the device node is missing, cannot be opened, the camera does not support frame‑size or interval enumeration, or the focus control is absent, and exit with a non‑zero status on any fatal error.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi that controls a camera pan‑tilt mount using two hobby servos driven over the GPIO hardware PWM bus, with four active‑low push‑buttons wired to ground and using the internal pull‑up resistors; the pan servo is connected to GPIO4 (BCM) and the tilt servo to GPIO5 (BCM), while the UP, DOWN, LEFT and RIGHT buttons are on GPIO6, GPIO7, GPIO8 and GPIO9 respectively, all using 50 Hz PWM where each loop iteration increments the pulse width by 10 µs and the loop delays 50 ms, the pulse widths must be clamped between 1000 µs (minimum) and 2000 µs (maximum) with a center position of 1500 µs, the program must initialize the driver library and check its return value, printing an error and exiting if initialization fails, output a startup message showing the pin assignments and the center position, respond to button presses by adjusting the appropriate servo pulse width in the allowed range, and install a SIGINT/SIGTERM handler that cleanly stops PWM on both servo pins using the library's API call, calls the library's API call() to release resources, and then exits.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that monitors an HC‑SR501 PIR sensor connected on the GPIO bus with its output tied to GPIO17 (BCM, physical pin 11), debounces each motion detection for two seconds, and otherwise polls the pin every 100 ms; when motion is detected the program must capture a JPEG snapshot from the Camera Module v2 at quality 85, store the file in a directory named motion_captures (creating the directory if necessary and handling an existing directory gracefully), then compose a JSON payload containing the filename, an ISO 8601 timestamp with microseconds, the motion status, and the GPIO pin number and POST this payload together with the image to an HTTP endpoint at http://<IP>:<port>/upload, where the IP address and port are supplied as command‑line arguments; the program must initialize the sensor driver and the HTTP library, configure GPIO17 as an input with a pull‑down resistor, check and report any initialization, system call, file, or network errors to stderr, and on receipt of SIGINT or SIGTERM perform a clean shutdown by releasing the driver, performing the required global cleanup of the HTTP library, and exiting, while ensuring the global HTTP library initialization is called exactly once at startup and the corresponding cleanup is called exactly once at exit.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that monitors the HC‑SR501 PIR sensor on the GPIO bus, using the sensor’s output connected to GPIO17 (BCM, physical pin 11) as an input with edge‑falling detection, implements a 50 ms debounce by waiting for a falling edge with a timeout, and upon a valid motion event invokes the camera capture utility with the options ‑o <filename> ‑‑width 640 ‑‑height 480 ‑q 85 ‑‑timeout 2000 ‑‑nopreview to produce a timestamped JPEG saved in /home/pi/images using the filename format YYYYMMDD_HHMMSS_mmm.jpg; each capture and any error from the capture command must be logged with a timestamp to /home/pi/motion_capture.log; the program must open the GPIO chip, claim GPIO17 as an input with edge‑falling (or edge‑rising) detection, check return codes of the capture command and log failures, and handle SIGINT and SIGTERM cleanly by releasing all driver library resources and closing file descriptors, while assuming the images directory already exists and avoiding any network publishing, ZeroMQ, or use of a driver library.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi (32‑bit or 64‑bit) that opens the USB UVC camera on /dev/video0, uses VIDIOC_QUERYCAP to verify the device, configures the capture to the documented V4L2_PIX_FMT_YUYV with V4L2_FIELD_NONE, requests a single memory‑mapped buffer, starts streaming, and then uses select() with a 2‑second timeout (retrying ioctl calls on EINTR) to wait for a frame; after a successful capture it must check that the returned width, height and pixel format match the requested values before processing, copy the complete YUYV macroblocks (Y0,U,Y1,V) to avoid color corruption, crop a 200 × 150 region, and write exactly 200*150*2 bytes to a file named cropped.yuv, checking the return value of every syscall, ioctl, mmap, fopen and fwrite and printing any errno with perror followed by EXIT_FAILURE on error; a SIGINT/SIGTERM handler must cleanly stop streaming, unmap the buffer, close the file descriptor and free any allocated memory.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that reads arrow‑key presses and a ‘q’ character from stdin, uses the GPIO hardware PWM bus to drive two SG90 servo motors—one pan servo attached to GPIO17 (BCM) and one tilt servo attached to GPIO18 (BCM)—operating at a 50 Hz frequency, initializing the driver library and exiting with code 1 after printing an error if initialization fails, starting both servos at a neutral 90‑degree position, moving each servo in 5‑degree steps in response to the appropriate arrow key while enforcing angle limits of 0 to 180 degrees and printing clear error messages for any out‑of‑range angle or PWM failure, inserting a 100 ms delay between successive commands, and handling cleanup by setting both servos to neutral, terminating the driver library cleanly, and exiting when a SIGINT signal is received or the user presses ‘q’.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that reads the CPU temperature from /sys/class/thermal/thermal_zone0/temp and parses the CPU usage percentage from /proc/stat, then renders both values once per second on an SSD1306 128×64 I2C OLED display attached to I2C bus 1, using a basic 5×7 bitmap font for text; the program must check every I2C write operation for errors, handle file‑read failures by returning specific error strings to be shown on the OLED, log any I2C communication failures to stderr and exit gracefully, and install a SIGINT handler to cleanly release all resources before termination.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that reads the pulse output of a YF‑S201 water flow sensor connected to GPIO17 (BCM numbering), computes the instantaneous flow rate and accumulates total volume, logs the current flow rate and total volume to the console once every second, and updates an HD44780 LCD attached via I2C bus 1 every ten seconds to display the same current flow rate and accumulated volume; the implementation must include robust error handling for any failures during GPIO initialization and must anticipate and manage possible I2C communication errors, and it must also catch SIGINT and SIGTERM signals to perform a graceful shutdown that releases all GPIO and I2C resources.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that reads an anemometer pulse on GPIO17 (BCM) using an interrupt on the rising edge, counts pulses over a 500 ms sample window to compute real‑time wind speed, and reads wind direction from a wind vane connected to channel 0 of an MCP3008 ADC on SPI0/CE0 in mode 0 at 1 MHz; the program must then update a 16x2 LCD with a PCF8574 backpack on I2C bus 1 to display both wind speed and direction every 500 ms, checking the result of every driver library, I2C and SPI call, detecting sensor‑absent conditions such as the ADC reading stuck at 0 or 1023 or any I2C/SPI failures and printing diagnostic messages to stderr while continuing to run, and finally handling SIGINT and SIGTERM to perform a graceful shutdown that releases the SPI handle, the I2C handle and any driver library resources, using the provided driver library’s I2C and SPI bit‑bang helpers or direct /dev/i2c and /dev/spidev access via its spi0SPIOpen call where appropriate.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that continuously reads proximity and ambient light data from a Silicon Labs Si1145 sensor attached to I2C bus 1, first verifying the sensor’s PART_ID before entering an infinite loop that samples the two measurements once per second, and logs each reading to a file named biometric_data.log in CSV format with an ISO‑8601 timestamp followed by the proximity value and the ambient light value, flushing the file after every write; the program must check the return code of every I2C read and write operation, handle cases where the sensor is absent or the bus reports errors in a graceful manner, and install a SIGINT handler that, upon termination, closes the I2C handle, closes the log file, and calls the sensor’s API call() function for proper cleanup.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that drives an HC‑SR04 ultrasonic sensor over GPIO, using GPIO 17 (BCM) as the TRIGGER output and GPIO 27 (BCM) as the ECHO input, with a 1 kΩ/2 kΩ voltage divider on the echo line to protect the 3.3 V‑tolerant pins from the sensor’s 5 V logic; the program must issue a 10 µs trigger pulse, then wait up to 30 ms for the echo rise and up to another 30 ms for the echo pulse width, compute the distance, reject any reading outside the 2‑400 cm range, and every 60 seconds log the result to a file named distance_log.txt with an ISO‑8601 timestamp, including explicit error or timeout entries, and if the measured distance is below 15 cm also log the message “Time to water the plant!”; all driver calls must be checked for failure, handling the sensor‑absent case where the echo never rises and the timeout case where the echo stays high, and the application must catch SIGINT and SIGTERM to perform a graceful shutdown that releases all resources and closes the log file.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the Adafruit APDS9960 sensor on I2C bus 1 to poll the device every 100 ms, detect proximity events and read the raw RGB color values, and whenever the proximity reading exceeds the threshold of 200 it appends a line containing the timestamp, the three RGB components and the proximity value to a CSV file named color_proximity_log.csv; the program must handle I2C communication errors by closing and reopening the bus and re‑initializing the sensor, and it must also catch SIGINT and SIGTERM signals to perform a graceful shutdown that closes the I2C handle, finalizes the CSV file, and releases any resources allocated by the driver.

prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that uses the I2C bus 1 to communicate with an Adafruit VL53L0X Time‑of‑Flight sensor, first verifying the sensor’s presence at the documented value before any initialization, then configuring a falling‑edge trigger input on GPIO 17 (BCM numbering) with a pull‑up resistor; the program must wait for each falling edge, trigger a single distance measurement, poll the RESULT_INTERRUPT_STATUS with approximately a 100 ms timeout, and upon successful read log a timestamped distance in millimetres to a file named distance_log.txt in CSV format as “timestamp,distance_mm”, while providing robust error handling for every I2C transaction, handling sensor‑absent conditions and timeout paths, and must also install a SIGINT handler that on receipt performs a graceful shutdown by closing the I2C handle, flushing and closing the log file, and releasing all driver library resources on every exit path, all without using the driver library.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the TDK CH101 ultrasonic sensor on I2C bus 1 to measure distance, waiting approximately 50 ms after each trigger before reading the result and sampling every 200 ms; the program must initialize the driver and open the I2C bus, verify each write and read operation as well as the file open for logging, and on any I2C error print a diagnostic message and skip to the next sample without crashing, while logging each successful reading in the format “YYYY‑MM‑DD HH:MM:SS, <distance_mm>” to a file named distance_log.txt and also printing the same line to stdout, using a fixed‑size local buffer for the timestamp to avoid dynamic allocation, and it must handle SIGINT (Ctrl‑C) gracefully by exiting the sampling loop, closing the I2C handle, the log file, and shutting down the driver cleanly.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses two TCRT5000 IR reflective sensors connected to the GPIO bus, with sensor 1 wired to GPIO 17 (BCM) and sensor 2 to GPIO 18 (BCM), to detect object proximity and log the binary readings (0 or 1) together with timestamps every 100 milliseconds to a file named obstacle_log.txt; the program must include robust error handling for any GPIO setup failures, and if a sensor read fails it should write an error message to stderr while continuing operation, and it must also handle SIGINT (Ctrl+C) to perform a graceful shutdown that releases all resources before exiting.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that continuously reads the distance from a TDK InvenSense ICU‑20201 ultrasonic Time‑of‑Flight sensor on I2C bus 1, sampling every 100 ms, and drives an LED connected to GPIO 17 (BCM numbering) such that the LED is turned on when the measured distance is below 20 cm and off otherwise, while logging each distance reading together with an ISO‑8601 timestamp to a file named distance_log.txt; the implementation must check the result of every I2C, driver library, and file operation, handle cases where the sensor is absent or the bus reports errors in a graceful manner, and ensure that all resources—including the I2C handle, the GPIO pin, and any driver state—are cleanly released on every exit path by handling SIGINT and SIGTERM signals.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that continuously reads proximity and ambient light data from a Silicon Labs Si1182‑GMR Optical Proximity and Ambient Light Sensor on I2C bus 1, sampling both measurements every 500 ms, and appends each reading with a timestamp to a file named biometric_log.txt; the implementation must check the return value of every I2C read and write operation, retry any failed read up to three times, and gracefully handle cases where the sensor is absent or the bus reports errors, while also installing a SIGINT (Ctrl+C) handler that cleanly releases the I2C handle, closes the log file, and terminates any driver resources before exiting.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that continuously reads distance measurements from a TDK InvenSense ICU-20201 ultrasonic Time‑of‑Flight sensor on I2C bus 1 at a 50 ms polling interval, lights an LED connected to GPIO 17 (BCM) whenever the measured distance falls below a configurable threshold (default 100 mm, supplied as the first command‑line argument), logs each reading with a timestamp to a file named “tof_log.txt”, verifies the sensor’s WHO_AM_I register during initialization, checks all I2C read/write return codes, gracefully handles sensor‑absent or bus‑error conditions without crashing, and ensures that on any exit path—including receipt of SIGINT—the program releases the I2C handle, resets the GPIO, and performs any required driver cleanup.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that communicates with an Omron B5L‑LD50‑07050 3D TOF sensor over the I2C bus (/dev/i2c-1) to detect intrusion events within 1 meter and log the average distance; the program must send the documented 4‑byte command frame to request a measurement, wait at least 10 ms before reading the documented 15‑byte response, verify that byte 0 matches the documented header value, extract the 16‑bit big‑endian distance from bytes 11 and 12, sample the sensor ten times per cycle with a 100 ms delay between cycles, compute the average distance, and when the average is less than 1000 mm write a timestamp and the average distance to a file named intrusion_log.txt; all I2C open, ioctl, read and write calls must be checked for failure, and the code must gracefully handle sensor‑absent (I2C NACK) and bus‑error conditions, while also installing a SIGINT handler so that pressing Ctrl‑C closes the I2C file descriptor and any open log files and releases all resources on every exit path.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that uses the I2C bus 1 to periodically read the distance from an Adafruit VL53L0X Time‑of‑Flight sensor, verifying the sensor’s presence at startup by reading its model ID register and confirming it matches the documented value, and exiting cleanly with an error message if the read fails or the ID mismatches; after successful initialization the program must poll the RESULT_INTERRUPT_STATUS with roughly a 100 ms timeout, obtain a distance measurement, and every 500 ms print to stdout a line formatted as “YYYY‑MM‑DD HH:MM:SS Distance: <N> mm”, while checking every I2C call for errors and printing strerror(errno) on failure, issuing a warning to stderr and continuing to the next iteration for any read/write error that occurs during the loop; the program must also handle SIGINT and SIGTERM gracefully by closing the I2C handle, invoking the library’s cleanup call, and exiting.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that periodically reads the 16‑bit proximity data from a Silicon Labs Si1182 optical sensor connected on I2C bus 1 (GPIO2 SDA / GPIO3 SCL) and logs the values to the console every 500 ms, while checking each driver library or I2C call for errors, detecting a sensor‑absent condition by a NACK on the initial write, handling any bus errors gracefully without crashing, and installing a SIGINT handler so that pressing Ctrl +C cleanly closes the I2C handle and invokes the library’s API call() for proper cleanup.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that opens the I2C bus 1 device file (/dev/i2c-1) with full error checking, sets the Melexis MLX75030 Time‑of‑Flight sensor as the I2C slave using ioctl I2C_SLAVE and verifies that the device responds, then enters a loop that every 500 ms (using nanosleep) reads the distance measurement from the sensor and prints a line to stdout in the form “Distance: <value> mm”; if an I2C read fails the program must write a diagnostic message to stderr and simply continue to the next cycle without exiting, while if the sensor is not present at startup it must print an error and exit with status 1; a SIGINT/SIGTERM handler must be installed so that pressing Ctrl‑C cleanly closes the I2C file descriptor and terminates the program with status 0.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that periodically reads the Texas Instruments OPT3101 Time‑of‑Flight sensor on I2C bus 1, logging every 500 ms the distance measurement from channel 0, the ambient light value, and any error flags to the console, while implementing robust error handling for I2C communication failures such as a missing sensor or bus errors and guaranteeing that all resources are cleanly released on every exit path, including a graceful shutdown when a SIGINT (Ctrl‑C) is received.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that periodically reads distance from an HC‑SR04 ultrasonic sensor connected on the GPIO bus, using GPIO 17 (BCM) as the trigger output and GPIO 18 (BCM) as the echo input, issuing a 10 µs trigger pulse each cycle, waiting up to 200 ms for the echo rising edge and up to 200 ms for the echo falling edge, and performing one read per second; each valid measurement must be logged to the console together with a timestamp, while the code must handle driver library initialization failure, echo‑edge timeouts, and invalid pulse durations (≤ 0 µs or > 38 ms, the HC‑SR04 maximum range timeout), include a comment noting that the HC‑SR04 operates at 5 V and the Pi GPIO is only 3.3 V tolerant and therefore a 1 kΩ resistor must be used on the echo line within the library’s API call() that provides microsecond precision, and finally ensure graceful shutdown on SIGINT or SIGTERM by invoking the library’s API call() on all exit paths.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that reads a range profile from a Texas Instruments IWR1443 mmWave radar over UART (/dev/serial0), decodes each data frame marked by an 8‑byte magic word header followed by 128 bytes of raw range profile data representing 64 little‑endian 16‑bit distance bins, checks whether any bin indicates a target within a 1.0‑meter distance threshold, and on detection logs an intrusion entry containing an ISO 8601 timestamp and the distance in meters to a comma‑separated file named intrusion_log.csv, while also activating an alert LED connected to GPIO 17 (BCM) for exactly 2 seconds; the program must handle UART initialization errors using the POSIX driver library, validate all I/O operations, gracefully manage sensor‑absent or bus‑error conditions, and ensure clean release of all resources on every exit path by handling SIGINT and SIGTERM.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that continuously reads obstacle detection data from an E18-D80NK IR sensor connected to GPIO 17, where the sensor presents an active‑low signal (0 when an obstacle is within the threshold distance and 1 otherwise), and drives a buzzer on GPIO 18 (active‑high) such that the buzzer is activated whenever an obstacle is detected and deactivated when the obstacle is removed; the program must poll the sensor every 100 ms via the GPIO bus, log each state transition with an ISO 8601 timestamp to a file named obstacle_log.txt, rigorously check all driver return values and handle any errors such as chip open failure, line request failure, or read/write errors, and also install handlers for SIGINT and SIGTERM to perform a graceful shutdown that releases all GPIO lines and closes the chip.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that interfaces with a TDK Chirp ICU-20201 ultrasonic time‑of‑flight sensor on I2C bus 1, reads the distance measurement every 100 ms, logs each distance together with an ISO 8601 timestamp to a file named distance_log.txt, and monitors the reading so that when the measured distance falls below 10.0 cm the program asserts a GPIO alert on physical pin 17 (BCM 17); the implementation must handle all I2C read/write errors, detect the absence of the sensor, and manage any errors that occur while creating or writing the log file, and it must also cleanly release all resources—including I2C handles, the GPIO pin, and any driver state—when receiving a SIGINT or SIGTERM signal.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that implements a parking‑assistance system using the STMicroelectronics VL53L1X Time‑of‑Flight sensor connected on I2C bus 1; the program must poll the sensor every 100 ms in the main loop, check the return code of every driver, I2C, and file operation, and for each measurement append a line “timestamp,distance_mm” to a file named distance_log.csv, creating the file with a header row “timestamp,distance_mm” only when it does not already exist, while also printing a parking guidance message to stdout based on the measured distance—‘STOP’ for less than 300 mm, ‘APPROACH’ for 300‑600 mm, ‘SLOW’ for 600‑1200 mm, and ‘CLEAR’ for greater than 1200 mm; the application must install handlers for SIGINT and SIGTERM to perform a graceful shutdown that releases the I2C handle, closes the log file, and de‑initialises the sensor driver on every exit path.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that reads the distance from a TDK InvenSense CH201 ultrasonic Time‑of‑Flight sensor on I2C bus 1 (GPIO 2/3 for SDA/SCL) every 100 ms, logs each timestamped distance and the corresponding LED blink frequency to stdout, and drives an LED connected to GPIO 18 (BCM) through a 330 Ω current‑limiting resistor to 3.3 V so that the LED blinks faster as the measured distance decreases, with each loop iteration performing exactly one half‑cycle of the LED blink (on or off) to keep the blinking smooth across samples; the program must check every driver and I2C call, retry any failed I2C read or write up to three times with 10 ms delays, and gracefully handle sensor‑absent conditions (I2C open failure) and bus‑error paths, and it must install SIGINT and SIGTERM handlers that on termination cleanly close the I2C handle, turn off the LED, and shut down the driver library.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that continuously reads distance data from a Melexis MLX75030 Time‑of‑Flight sensor on I2C bus 1 at a 100 ms sampling interval, triggering each measurement with the required write command, waiting the appropriate delay, then reading the 2‑byte distance value in centimeters, and appending each reading to a comma‑separated file named distance_log.csv formatted as “timestamp,distance_cm”; the program must include robust error handling for I2C communication failures such as sensor absence, bus errors, or read/write timeouts, implement retry logic for transient errors, log any errors to stderr, and ensure clean resource release on all exit paths, including graceful termination when receiving SIGINT or SIGTERM.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that interfaces two TCRT5000 IR obstacle avoidance sensors on the GPIO bus, connecting sensor 1 to GPIO 17 (physical pin 11, BCM) and sensor 2 to GPIO 27 (physical pin 13, BCM), polls each sensor every 10 ms, applies a 50 ms software debounce per sensor, and logs every state transition to a file named proximity_log.txt with an ISO 8601 UTC timestamp, the sensor ID (1 or 2), and the event type ('DETECTED' for a HIGH‑to‑LOW transition indicating an obstacle and 'CLEARED' for a LOW‑to‑HIGH transition indicating clearance); the program must check the return values of the library’s API call() three times as required, verify all file I/O operations, and on all exit paths—including graceful shutdown on SIGINT or SIGTERM—ensure clean resource release by closing the log file and calling the library’s API call() to release the GPIO resources.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that continuously measures distance from a TDK CH‑101 Time‑of‑Flight sensor connected on I2C bus 1 (/dev/i2c‑1) by opening the I2C device with open(2), setting the slave address with ioctl(I2C_SLAVE), and using a helper that performs a combined write‑then‑read transaction to poll the MEAS_STATUS register with a 50 ms timeout before reading a successful distance measurement; after each successful read the program must wait 500 ms before the next sample, log an ISO‑8601 timestamp and the distance in millimetres to a CSV file named “distance_log.csv” with columns timestamp,distance_mm, checking the result of every open, ioctl, read, write and fopen call and, on any I2C failure, printing a diagnostic message including errno to stderr and skipping that sample without crashing; the application must also install handlers for SIGINT and SIGTERM that cleanly close the I2C file descriptor, flush and close the CSV file, and then exit.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that periodically reads zone distance data from a VL53L5CX ToF sensor connected on the I2C bus (/dev/i2c-1), configures the sensor for an 8×8 zone grid (64 zones), and logs all 64 zone distances to the console every 500 ms; the implementation must perform all I2C register reads and writes manually using standard Linux file I/O without any external driver library, include robust error handling for both I2C communication and sensor initialization, and ensure clean resource release on all exit paths, including handling of SIGINT.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that periodically reads distance measurements from a Melexis MLX75030 Time‑of‑Flight sensor on I2C bus 1, sampling the distance every 100 ms and logging each measurement to the console together with a millisecond timestamp; the implementation must check the return values of all driver initialization and I2C read/write calls, retry any failed I2C transaction up to three times with a 10 ms delay between attempts, and gracefully handle cases where the sensor is absent or the bus reports errors, while also ensuring that on all exit paths—including a graceful shutdown triggered by SIGINT (Ctrl‑C)—the I2C handle is closed and the driver library is properly terminated.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that reads distance data from a VL53L4CX time‑of‑flight sensor connected on I2C bus 1, polls the sensor’s interrupt status register every 500 ms, and logs each valid measurement to the console with a microsecond‑precision timestamp formatted as “Timestamp: YYYY‑MM‑DD HH:MM:SS.uuuuuu, Distance: N mm”; the implementation must perform full error checking on every driver library and I2C call, verify the return value of each I2C write and abort cleanly on failure, skip a cycle without reporting an error if the interrupt status bit is not set after the poll, print an error to stderr and continue to the next cycle for transient I2C communication failures while aborting cleanly for initialization failures, use the driver library for I2C rather than the generic driver library and address the specified registers directly, and install handlers for SIGINT and SIGTERM that close the I2C handle, invoke the library’s cleanup API call, and exit with return 0, ensuring that all resources are released on every exit path.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the VL53L1X time‑of‑flight sensor on I2C bus 1 to trigger distance readings every 500 ms, configures the sensor for continuous ranging mode, and activates a buzzer connected to GPIO 22 (BCM, active) whenever the measured distance falls below 100 mm; the program must handle I2C errors gracefully by logging the error and skipping the current iteration, and it must ensure clean resource release on all exit paths, including handling SIGINT for a graceful shutdown.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that implements a parking‑assist system using an HC‑SR04 ultrasonic sensor and an SG90 servo connected on the GPIO bus, with the trigger line on GPIO 23 (BCM), the echo line on GPIO 24 (BCM) and the servo control line on GPIO 17 (BCM); the program must initialize the driver library and verify success, then repeatedly issue a 10 µs trigger pulse, wait for the echo while treating any condition where the echo line remains low or high for more than 50 ms as a sensor timeout that returns a sentinel error value and causes the reading to be skipped, map valid distances from 2 cm to 400 cm linearly to the servo angle range of –90° to +90° (2 cm → –90°, 400 cm → +90°) and invoke the library’s API call to set that angle, log each successful distance reading with a timestamp to a file named sensor_data.log appending each entry, run this loop every 200 ms until interrupted, and install SIGINT and SIGTERM handlers that on receipt stop the library’s API call (pulse 0), release all resources and invoke the library’s API call on every exit path, ensuring that no GPIO operations occur after the library’s API call and that only valid BCM GPIO numbers are used (avoiding GPIO 28).

prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that measures distance with an HC‑SR04 ultrasonic sensor using a falling‑edge interrupt on the echo pin over the GPIO bus, configuring TRIG on GPIO 23 (physical pin 16, BCM, output, initially LOW) and ECHO on GPIO 24 (physical pin 18, BCM, input, pull‑down) while noting in a comment that the ECHO line is 5 V and must be level‑shifted or divided for the Pi’s 3.3 V tolerance; the program must generate a 10 µs trigger pulse every 200 ms (5 Hz sampling), register an alert callback that captures both rising and falling edge timestamps in microseconds, compute the pulse duration as falling_tick minus rising_tick while handling the driver’s 32‑bit tick wraparound (~72 min), reject any measured pulse width below 100 µs (noise) or above 30 000 µs (timeout/no object) and log such rejections as warnings, treat the absence of a valid echo within 60 ms of triggering as a timeout warning, and for each valid reading log the distance with an ISO 8601 timestamp to both stdout and an append‑mode file named distance_log.txt, flushing after each write; the program must initialize the driver library with full error checking, printing a diagnostic and exiting with a non‑zero status on failure, and must handle SIGINT and SIGTERM to perform a clean shutdown by closing the log file, releasing GPIO resources via the library’s API call, and exiting cleanly.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that implements a smart parking gate using a VL53L1X time‑of‑flight sensor and a servo motor, connecting the sensor on I2C bus 1 (GPIO2/SDA, GPIO3/SCL) with its shutdown line tied to GPIO23 (BCM) and its interrupt line to GPIO24 (BCM), and driving the servo with hardware PWM on GPIO18 (BCM); the program must verify the VL53L1X model ID during initialization, check every I2C read and write for errors, handle cases where the sensor is absent or the bus fails, open the gate when an object is detected within 50 cm and close it when the distance exceeds 60 cm to provide hysteresis, log each gate state change together with a timestamp and the measured distance to a file named parking_log.txt, and ensure that all resources are cleanly released on any exit path by installing SIGINT and SIGTERM signal handlers.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that continuously polls a VL53L1X time‑of‑flight sensor on I2C bus 1 every 500 ms, initializes the sensor with a soft reset, configures its timing budget, and starts ranging, then uses the 16‑bit register access functions provided by the sensor’s driver to read distance measurements and opens the gate (GPIO 18 HIGH, GPIO 19 LOW) when an object is detected within 20 cm (200 mm) and closes it (GPIO 18 LOW, GPIO 19 HIGH) otherwise, logging each open or close event with an ISO 8601 UTC timestamp to a file named gate_events.log, checking all driver and I2C return codes and handling sensor‑absent or bus‑error conditions gracefully by logging the error, and implementing SIGINT/SIGTERM signal handling to ensure that on any exit path the I2C handle is closed, the GPIO pins are reset, the log file is closed, and the appropriate library cleanup API is called.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses I2C bus 1 to communicate with a VL53L1X time‑of‑flight sensor and controls a DC motor on GPIO17 (forward) and GPIO18 (backward) according to distance thresholds, triggering a distance reading on each rising edge of GPIO24 (BCM) via a pigpio ISR, where distances below 100 mm cause the motor to run forward, distances above 300 mm cause it to run backward, and values in between stop the motor, while logging every distance measurement and any motor state change to the console; the program must perform the VL53L1X register sequence of a soft reset write, a 1 ms delay, a start‑measurement write, then poll the status register until the data‑ready bit is set before reading the 16‑bit distance value, must check all driver and I2C return values, retry failed I2C transactions with exponential backoff, safely stop the motor if the sensor is absent or a bus error occurs, and on receipt of SIGINT or SIGTERM cleanly release resources by closing I2C handles, stopping the motor, and invoking the sensor’s API cleanup call.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that implements a proximity‑based interactive art installation using an MPR121 capacitive touch sensor connected on the I2C bus (/dev/i2c-1, GPIO 2/SDA and GPIO 3/SCL); the program must poll the touch status registers every 50 ms, monitor all twelve electrodes (ELE0‑ELE11), and when any electrode detects proximity it should drive a distinct 4‑bit LED pattern on GPIO 17 (BCM) as bit 0, GPIO 18 as bit 1, GPIO 27 as bit 2, and GPIO 22 as bit 3, while logging every proximity event to the console with a timestamp; it must validate every I2C read and write, verify the sensor is present by reading back a known register after a soft reset, and gracefully handle sensor‑absent or bus‑error conditions, and finally ensure clean resource release on all exit paths by releasing all GPIO lines, closing the I2C and log file descriptors, and installing signal handlers for SIGINT and SIGTERM.

prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that implements a capacitive touch‑based proximity detector using an MPR121 connected on I2C bus 1, reads the device ID to verify the sensor is present, configures all required MPR121 registers including FFI, SFI, ESI, debounce, AFE configuration and baseline filtering, monitors the touch inputs for a proximity event, and when such an event is detected turns an LED wired to GPIO 27 (BCM numbering) on for exactly one second, logs the proximity event with a timestamp to a file named proximity.log, handles any I2C communication errors gracefully, and ensures that all resources are cleanly released when the program receives a SIGINT or SIGTERM signal.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that measures distance using an HC‑SR04 ultrasonic sensor connected on the GPIO bus with the trigger line wired to GPIO17 (BCM, output) and the echo line to GPIO18 (BCM, input); the program must hold the trigger low for 5 µs, then pulse it high for 10 µs before returning it low, wait up to 30 ms for the echo rising edge, then measure the echo pulse width with a further 30 ms timeout, compute distance using the speed of sound ≈ 343 m/s at 20 °C, reject any reading outside the 2‑400 cm range and log an error line instead, and otherwise write a line to a file named distance_log.txt every second containing an ISO 8601 UTC timestamp and the measured distance, flushing after each write; each access to the trigger and echo pins must include proper error checking, sensor‑absent conditions (echo never rises) and timeout paths must be handled explicitly, a SIGINT handler must be installed that sets a volatile sig_atomic_t flag, and on receipt of SIGINT the program must release all driver resources, close the log file and exit cleanly without leaking resources on any exit path.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that measures distance with an HC‑SR04 ultrasonic sensor using an interrupt‑driven echo pulse‑width measurement on the GPIO bus, with TRIG connected to GPIO17 (BCM) and ECHO connected to GPIO18 (BCM) through a 1 kΩ/2 kΩ voltage divider to keep the Pi input at ~3.3 V, generating a 10 µs trigger pulse once per second, capturing the echo pulse width via an ISR callback on either‑edge transitions, validating that the pulse width is greater than zero and falls within a sane range (approximately 58 µs to 25 ms, corresponding to about 1 cm to 4 m) while handling tick wrap‑around, converting the measured time to meters, and appending each reading together with a timestamp to a file named distance_log.txt; the program must check that the driver library initializes correctly and that the log file opens successfully, and it must install a SIGINT/SIGTERM handler that cleanly shuts down by disabling the ISR, closing the log file, and invoking the library’s cleanup API call, with no use of UDP networking or any other external communication.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that interfaces with a VL53L1X time‑of‑flight sensor on I2C bus 1 using the documented address, controls the sensor’s XSHUT pin with GPIO27 (BCM) configured as an output and set high to enable the sensor (active‑low trigger), repeatedly reads the distance every 100 ms, and logs each reading to the systemd journal via syslog including a timestamp, the measured distance in millimetres, and the sensor status, using LOG_INFO for successful reads and LOG_ERR for any read failures; the program must verify that the driver library initializes correctly and that the I2C device can be opened, handle read errors by logging them and continuing the loop without crashing, and install SIGINT and SIGTERM handlers that close the I2C handle, terminate the driver library, and exit cleanly.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that uses a VL53L1X time‑of‑flight sensor on I2C bus 1 (using the documented address) to poll distance measurements every 100 ms, converts the 16‑bit register value from millimetres to centimetres, and controls a gate actuator connected to GPIO24 (BCM, active‑high) so that the gate is opened when the measured distance is less than 20 cm and closed otherwise, initializing the gate to the closed state (GPIO24 low) at startup; the program must log each distance reading, each gate state change, and any errors with timestamps to a file named “gate_log.txt”, perform error handling for all I2C operations, sensor initialization, and file operations, and include a SIGINT/SIGTERM handler that gracefully shuts down by closing the I2C interface, closing the log file, and terminating the driver library.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that measures distance with an HC‑SR04 ultrasonic sensor using an interrupt‑driven echo timing callback and pans an SG90 servo motor via the library’s API call to track it, logging timestamp, distance in centimeters, and the API call angle in degrees to a file named distance_log.csv with a header row and flushing after each write; the HC‑SR04 trigger pin is connected to GPIO23 (BCM) and must be pulsed high for 10 µs every 100 ms, the echo pin is on GPIO24 (BCM) and must be timed with a 30 ms timeout using the 32‑bit tick counter with wrap‑around handling, while the SG90 servo is driven from GPIO18 (BCM, hardware PWM‑capable) and its angle is set through the API call; the program must check driver initialization, alert registration, API call return codes, and file opening, and on an invalid distance reading (out of the 2‑400 cm range or no echo) it must log –1.0 and command the servo to 90 degrees; distance readings are to be filtered with a 5‑sample moving average, and the shared pulse‑width data between the interrupt callback and the main loop must be protected by a flag‑based handshake where the callback sets pulse_width and a new_pulse flag and the main thread reads and clears it; a volatile sig_atomic_t flag must be used to catch SIGINT, upon which the program stops the servo by issuing the API call with 0, closes the CSV file, and calls the API cleanup function before exiting.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that communicates with a VL53L1X time‑of‑flight sensor on I2C bus 1 using the documented address, reads a distance measurement every 50 ms, stores each reading in millimetres in a circular buffer holding the last ten values, and drives a warning LED connected to GPIO17 (BCM) high whenever a reading falls below 200 mm and low otherwise; the implementation must follow the recommended STMicroelectronics initialization sequence—set the default configuration, enable signal‑rate checking, configure cross‑talk compensation, and start ranging—while checking every I2C read and write for errors, handling sensor initialization failures, printing any read error and continuing operation, and providing a SIGINT handler that cleanly shuts down by turning off the LED, closing the I2C interface, terminating the driver usage, and releasing all resources on any exit path, using only modern APIs.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that interfaces with a Silicon Labs Si1102 proximity sensor on I2C bus 1 using the documented address, configures the sensor’s proximity interrupt to GPIO27 (BCM numbering) on a rising edge, and on each interrupt reads the 16‑bit proximity value, compares it to a threshold (default 1000 but overrideable with a command‑line option “‑t <threshold>”), and appends a line to a file named proximity.log containing the current timestamp in “YYYY‑MM‑DD HH:MM:SS” format, the raw proximity reading, and the status string “SAFE” if the value is less than or equal to the threshold or “ALERT” if it exceeds the threshold; the program must also accept an optional “‑a <i2c_address>” argument to set the I2C address in hex or decimal, must initialise the I2C interface and GPIO with full error checking, must verify every I2C transaction, GPIO setup, and file operation and print any errors to stderr, must implement a thread‑safe interrupt handler that does not perform blocking calls (using a flag or queue to defer processing), and must install a SIGINT handler that on receipt cleanly shuts down by closing the I2C device, closing the log file, and terminating the sensor driver, while using the provided driver facilities for GPIO and I2C but not for higher‑level sensor handling.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that reads distance from an HC‑SR04 ultrasonic sensor and drives an 8‑ohm speaker as a theremin‑like instrument, using the hardware‑timed PWM on PWM0 (GPIO18, BCM) to generate audio tones whose pitch is controlled by the measured distance; the HC‑SR04 trigger line must be pulsed for 10 µs on GPIO23 (BCM) and the echo line read on GPIO24 (BCM) with a timeout of 200 ms, mapping distances from 2 cm to 200 cm to frequencies between 200 Hz and 2000 Hz on a logarithmic scale with a 50 % duty cycle, while performing robust error checking on every driver API call and, if a distance is out of range or a timeout occurs, preserving the previous frequency, and installing a SIGINT/SIGTERM handler that cleanly stops the PWM and terminates the driver, ensuring all resources are released on exit.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that synthesizes a theremin‑like instrument using a piezo buzzer whose pitch is controlled by the distance measured with an HC‑SR04 ultrasonic sensor; the buzzer is connected to PWM0 on GPIO18 (BCM), the HC‑SR04 trigger line to GPIO23 (BCM) and the echo line to GPIO24 (BCM) with a pull‑down resistor, and the program must initialize the driver library, verify that the GPIO modes are correctly set, then in a loop trigger the sensor with a low‑initial state followed by a 10 µs high pulse, measure the echo pulse width with microsecond precision using the library’s timing API, enforce an echo timeout of 100 ms (reporting an error and reusing the last valid distance if exceeded), wait 10 ms between readings, map the practical distance range of 5 cm to 50 cm linearly to a frequency range of 200 Hz to 2000 Hz (clamping outside values), generate a continuous tone on the buzzer using the library’s frequency generation API (not raw PWM), print both the measured distance and the resulting frequency to the console each iteration, handle any sensor read failures gracefully, and install a SIGINT handler that stops the PWM and shuts down the driver library cleanly on program termination.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that continuously measures the distance to the nearest object using an HC‑SR04 ultrasonic sensor, triggering the sensor on GPIO17 (BCM) with a 10 µs pulse and reading the echo on GPIO18 (BCM) with a 50 ms timeout, looping every 500 ms; the program must initialise the driver library, configure the trigger pin as an output initially low and the echo pin as an input, check that the driver library initialisation succeeds, obtain each echo pulse duration, convert it to a distance in centimeters, reject any reading below 2 cm or above 400 cm and print “Invalid reading” for those, otherwise print the valid distance as “Distance: X.XX cm”, and if the distance is below 10 cm also print “Too close!”; it must handle a timeout from the echo measurement by treating it as a –1 result, and it must install a SIGINT handler that sets a flag to exit the loop, then terminates the driver library and releases all resources before exiting cleanly.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that interfaces with a TDK InvenSense ICU-20201 ultrasonic time‑of‑flight sensor over SPI (mode 0, 1 MHz clock) using the chip‑select line on GPIO8 (BCM, CE0), continuously reads the distance for an obstacle‑avoidance application with a 100 ms delay between readings, and appends each timestamp and distance value in millimetres (range 200‑5000 mm) to a file named distance_log.csv opened in append mode; the program must use the sensor driver’s API call for SPI read operations, handle SPI communication errors, sensor initialization failures, and sensor‑absent conditions gracefully by logging errors to stderr while continuing to run indefinitely, and install a SIGINT/SIGTERM handler that closes the SPI handle, releases all resources, and flushes and closes the CSV log file on exit.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that reads temperature from an Analog Devices TMP05 digital temperature sensor by polling its PWM‑style output on GPIO4 (BCM, physical pin 7), measuring the high‑pulse width and total cycle width with a busy‑wait loop using microsecond‑resolution timestamps obtained from the library’s call() API, sampling once every 5 seconds and applying a 50 ms timeout on each edge wait; the program must verify that the driver library initializes correctly and that the log file “temperature_log.txt” opens in append mode, compute the temperature while guarding against division by zero if the low‑time (TL) is zero, flag any reading outside the valid range of –40 °C to +150 °C as an error, and after three consecutive failures write a “SENSOR MALFUNCTION” entry to the log, logging each valid reading together with an ISO‑8601 timestamp; it must also handle SIGINT and SIGTERM to perform a clean shutdown by closing the file and releasing the driver library resources.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that reads temperature and humidity from a Sensirion SHT35‑DIS‑B sensor on I2C bus 1 using the documented high‑repeatability, clock‑stretching‑disabled measurement command, validates the 8‑bit CRC for both the temperature and humidity words, and, after waiting at least 15 ms for the 6‑byte result, converts the raw values to degrees Celsius and percent relative humidity with the standard Sensirion formulas, then adds a sinusoidal offset of ±2 °C and ±5 % RH over a one‑hour period to simulate a greenhouse environment before logging each reading with an ISO‑8601 UTC timestamp to a file named “environmental_data.txt” every 5 seconds; if any I2C read/write or CRC check fails, the program must retry up to three times with a one‑second delay and, after exhausting retries, log NaN values, while also providing robust error handling for driver initialization, I2C open/read/write, and file open, and must handle SIGINT and SIGTERM to gracefully shut down by closing the I2C handle, flushing and closing the log file, and terminating the driver cleanly.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that interfaces with the Sensirion SDP810-125Pa differential pressure sensor on I2C bus 1 using the documented I2C address, sends the documented continuous measurement command, waits the approximately 45 ms conversion time, then reads the 9‑byte block containing pressure, temperature and scale factor each followed by an 8‑bit CRC‑8 checksum (using the polynomial and initial value documented for the sensor), validates those CRCs, converts the raw data to pressure in pascals and temperature in degrees Celsius with the sensor‑specified formulas, and logs a timestamp together with the pressure and temperature values to a CSV file named “airflow.csv” at a rate of one entry per second; the program must also detect and handle sensor‑absent or bus‑error conditions, and on receipt of SIGINT or SIGTERM perform a graceful shutdown that closes the I2C file descriptor and any open file handles.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that continuously reads temperature and humidity from a Sensirion SHT35‑DIS‑B sensor on I2C bus 1 using the documented single‑shot high‑repeatability measurement command with clock‑stretching disabled, waiting at least 15 ms after issuing the command before reading the six‑byte result, sampling every five seconds, validating both CRC‑8 checksums with the documented polynomial and initial value, and logging each reading to a CSV file named environment.csv with an ISO‑8601 timestamp followed by temperature in Celsius and relative humidity in percent, inserting a header row if the file does not already exist or is empty; the program must check the driver initialization, opening of the I2C bus, every I2C read/write operation, CRC validation, and file opening, printing a descriptive error to stderr on any failure and either continuing or exiting as appropriate, and it must install a SIGINT/SIGTERM handler that performs a clean shutdown by closing the I2C handle and invoking the sensor library’s shutdown call.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that periodically reads temperature and humidity from an Adafruit Si7021 temperature and humidity sensor on I2C bus 1 (GPIO 2/3) using the documented I2C address, polling each measurement until data is available or a 100 ms timeout expires, reading three bytes (MSB, LSB, CRC) for each value and verifying the CRC‑8 checksum with the documented polynomial and initial value, logging a line every 5 seconds to a CSV file named environment.log with a header “timestamp,temperature_C,humidity_percent” and ISO‑8601 timestamps, writing “ERROR” in place of the numeric fields together with a descriptive message to stderr whenever an I2C or CRC error occurs, checking the return value of every system call, handling sensor‑absent conditions such as I2C open failure or NACK, and on any read failure issuing the documented sensor reset command before the next cycle; the program must also install a SIGINT/SIGTERM handler that cleanly closes the I2C file descriptor and exits gracefully, thereby simulating a greenhouse monitoring system.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that reads differential pressure and temperature from a Sensirion SDP810-500Pa sensor on I2C bus 1 using the documented I2C address, initiates continuous measurement with the documented command, waits the required conversion time, then reads the 9‑byte response containing pressure MSB, pressure LSB, CRC, temperature MSB, temperature LSB, CRC and three scale‑factor bytes, validates the CRC‑8 for both pressure and temperature raw values, converts the raw data to floating‑point pressure (Pa) and temperature (°C), and logs each sample once per second to a binary file named airflow.dat with pressure followed by temperature as floats while keeping the file handle open across samples; the program must check driver initialization, I2C opening, command write and read results, handle sensor‑absent and bus‑error conditions, and implement signal handling for SIGINT and SIGTERM to perform a graceful shutdown that closes the I2C handle, terminates the driver, and closes the file on all exit paths.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that reads differential pressure from a Sensirion SDP800-500Pa sensor over I2C bus 1 using the documented I2C address, sends the documented continuous measurement command, waits the documented conversion time of 45 ms, then reads the 9‑byte response (three data words each followed by a CRC‑8 byte) and validates each CRC‑8 with the documented polynomial; the program must log each pressure reading together with a timestamp to a file named pressure_log.txt every 5 seconds, handle any I2C write or read errors, CRC failures, or the sensor being absent without crashing, and on receipt of SIGINT or SIGTERM cleanly close the I2C handle, flush and close the log file, and terminate the driver library gracefully for use in a DIY ventilation system.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that reads the differential pressure from a Honeywell Zephyr HAF Series HAFBLF0100A2AX5 digital airflow sensor over the I2C bus, samples the sensor every 100 ms, computes the corresponding flow rate, and drives a PWM fan connected to GPIO18 (BCM numbering) using hardware PWM at a frequency of 25 kHz, while logging each measurement to a file named flow_log.txt in the format “timestamp,pressure_Pa\n”; the program must include robust handling of I2C communication failures by logging errors to stderr without crashing, and must clean up gracefully on receipt of SIGINT or SIGTERM by turning off the fan, closing the I2C handle, flushing and closing the log file, and terminating the driver library.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that continuously reads pressure and temperature from an STMicroelectronics LPS33HW pressure sensor on the I2C bus, sampling once per second using the sensor’s API call, and logs each reading to a file named environmental_data.txt in the format “YYYY‑MM‑DD HH:MM:SS, Pressure: XXXX.XX hPa, Temperature: XX.XX °C” by converting the current time with localtime_r; the program must check the return value of every I2C read and write operation, and on any failure write a timestamped error message to both stderr and the log file while continuing the loop, flush the log file after each write, and handle graceful termination on SIGINT by setting a volatile sig_atomic_t flag, then closing the I2C handle, closing the log file, and invoking the library’s cleanup call before exiting.

/*
 * greenhouse_monitor.c — Raspberry Pi Zero W + Adafruit TMP117
 *
 * Wiring:
 *   TMP117 SDA  -> GPIO2 (pin 3, I2C bus 1)
 *   TMP117 SCL  -> GPIO3 (pin 5, I2C bus 1)
 *   TMP117 VDD  -> 3.3 V
 *   TMP117 GND  -> GND
 *
 * Build:
 *   gcc -O2 -Wall -Wextra -o greenhouse_monitor greenhouse_monitor.c
 *
 * TMP117 registers (16-bit, little-endian on the wire):
 *   0x00  T0_OUT_L  (T_out LSB)
 *   0x01  T0_OUT_H  (T_out MSB)
 *   0x02  T0_CFG    (T_out config)
 *   0x03  T0_INT_EN (T0 interrupt enable)
 *   0x04  T0_INT_STA (T0 interrupt status)
 *   0x05  T0_INT_CLR (T0 interrupt clear)
 *   0x06  T0_T0_CFG (T0 config)
 *   0x07  T0_T1_CFG (T1 config)
 *   0x08  T0_T1_OUT_L (T1_OUT LSB)
