prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that continuously reads temperature from a Texas Instruments TMP117 high‑accuracy temperature sensor on the I2C bus, sampling once per second and appending each reading to a file named temperature_log.txt using the exact format “YYYY‑MM‑DD HH:MM:SS, Temperature: <value> C\n”, while checking the return value of every I2C call, handling both sensor‑absent and bus‑error conditions, attempting to re‑initialize the I2C handle up to three consecutive times on failure before exiting, correctly processing negative temperature values, and ensuring that on receipt of SIGINT (Ctrl+C) the program closes the I2C handle and terminates the driver cleanly on all exit paths.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that continuously reads airflow data from a Honeywell HAF Series HAFUHH0025PA3 flow sensor over the I2C bus, sampling once every second, extracting a 14‑bit flow value and a 12‑bit temperature value from a single 4‑byte read using the sensor’s API call (no register pointer write required), handling the first two reads after power‑up which may return stale data, and writing each timestamped measurement in SLPM and °C to a file named flow_log.txt; the program must detect I2C communication failures such as sensor disconnection or bus errors, log any read error, attempt to re‑initialize the I2C handle, and on receipt of SIGINT or SIGTERM cleanly close the I2C handles, close the log file, and terminate the driver library.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that bit‑bangs a single‑wire DHT11 temperature/humidity sensor on GPIO4 (BCM, physical pin 7) using the provided API call for microsecond timing, the provided API call for GPIO direction control, the provided API call for reading and writing pin levels, and the provided API call for clean shutdown; the program must generate the start signal by pulling the line low for at least 18 ms, then releasing it so the sensor can respond with an 80 µs low pulse followed by an 80 µs high pulse, after which each of the 40 data bits is transmitted beginning with a 50 µs low period and a high period of about 26‑28 µs for a ‘0’ or about 70 µs for a ‘1’, sampling the sensor no more often than every 2 seconds (the DHT11 minimum interval is 1 s), decode the 40 bits into humidity integer (byte 0), humidity decimal (byte 1, always 0), temperature integer (byte 2), temperature decimal (byte 3, always 0) and verify the checksum, write each successful reading to a file named dht11_readings.txt with an ISO‑8601 timestamp, detect and log timeouts on the start signal, response, and each data bit as well as checksum failures and sensor‑absent conditions such as a line stuck high or low, recording each error with a timestamp and a status code, and on receipt of SIGINT or SIGTERM release the GPIO resources via the library’s cleanup API, close any open file handles, and exit gracefully.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that reads temperature and humidity from an Adafruit SHT31-D sensor on the I2C bus using SDA on GPIO2 (BCM, bus 1) and SCL on GPIO3 (BCM, bus 1), waiting at least 15 ms after issuing the measurement command and logging a new reading every 5 seconds to a file named sht31d_data.log with ISO‑8601 timestamps in the format “YYYY‑MM‑DD HH:MM:SS,temperature,humidity”, while checking that the driver library initializes correctly, that the I2C interface opens, that the log file opens, and that each I2C write, I2C read and CRC‑8 validation (using the documented polynomial and initial value) succeed, retrying any failed I2C transaction up to three times and, if the sensor continues to fail, logging the error with a timestamp and continuing operation, and finally handling SIGINT or SIGTERM by closing the I2C handle, closing the log file, and terminating the driver library; the program must read exactly six bytes per measurement (two bytes temperature plus one CRC, two bytes humidity plus one CRC) and validate each CRC‑8 as specified.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that reads two Analog Devices ADPD105 photometric front‑end sensors on the I2C bus, computes the correlated color temperature (CCT) from the sensor data, and logs the average CCT once per second to a file named cct_log.csv, creating the file with a header line “Timestamp,Average_CCT” if it does not already exist; the implementation must use the sensor’s API calls or equivalent block reads for register access, verify the success of every I2C read and write operation, and on any sensor‑absent or bus‑error condition gracefully log an error to stderr and skip that cycle’s entry, while ensuring that all I2C handles, file streams and any driver resources are cleanly released on every exit path, including handling of SIGINT and SIGTERM signals.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that continuously reads the absolute pressure and temperature from a Melexis MLX90824 absolute pressure sensor over the I2C bus, performing a read cycle every 2 seconds, and appends each measurement together with an ISO‑8601 timestamp to a file named pressure_log.txt; the program must check the result of every driver library or I2C call, and if the sensor is absent, the bus reports an error, or a read fails, it must log the error with a timestamp instead of silently skipping, and it must ensure that on all exit paths—including normal termination, SIGINT, and SIGTERM—it cleanly releases resources by closing the I2C handle, closing the log file, and invoking the sensor library’s cleanup API, while running indefinitely until interrupted.

prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that continuously reads the TDK ICP-10125 barometric pressure sensor over I2C, retrieving exactly six bytes per read (two pressure bytes, two temperature bytes, and two CRC bytes) while checking every I2C syscall for errors, handling sensor‑absent or bus‑error conditions, and verifying the CRC on each sensor read; after each trigger a 20 ms delay must be observed, the sensor should be polled once per second, and the result used to drive a warning LED connected to GPIO17 (BCM) where the LED blinks at 1 Hz (500 ms on, 500 ms off) under normal conditions and switches to a 5 Hz pattern (100 ms on, 100 ms off) whenever the measured pressure falls below 95 000 Pa, with the GPIO line requested, set to output, and toggled accordingly; the program must also install a SIGINT handler that safely closes the I2C file descriptor and releases the GPIO line before exiting.
pinned_library: Linux i2c-dev for I2C, libgpiod for GPIO

prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that reads ambient and object temperature from a Melexis MLX90614ESF-BAA infrared temperature sensor over the I2C bus, logs the timestamped readings to a file named temperature_log.txt every 2 seconds, and controls a cooling fan connected to GPIO18 (BCM) with hysteresis so that the fan turns on when the object temperature exceeds 30 °C and turns off when it falls below 28 °C; the program must validate driver library initialization, opening the I2C bus, and each I2C read/write operation, retrying any failed read up to three times with a 10 ms delay between attempts and skipping logging for invalid readings, and it must handle SIGINT and SIGTERM by closing the I2C handle, turning off the fan, and terminating the driver library.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that continuously reads the Sensirion SHT40 sensor on I2C bus 1, issuing the measurement command, waiting at least 10 ms, then reading exactly six bytes, and streams the live temperature and humidity values to a local HTTP server on port 8080 using the library’s API call to serve an HTML page that displays the current temperature and humidity while clamping humidity to the range 0‑100 %; the implementation must include robust error handling for I2C communication such as sensor absence or bus errors with up to three retries per read, and must cleanly release all resources on every exit path, handling SIGINT and SIGTERM signals appropriately.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that reads temperature from a Texas Instruments TMP102 on I2C bus 1 using the documented address, performs a measurement every 5 seconds, and appends each result to a timestamped CSV file named temperature_log.csv with lines formatted as “YYYY‑MM‑DD HH:MM:SS,XX.XX”; the program must include standard headers such as errno.h and stdint.h to compile without warnings, check the success of all initialization and I/O calls, log any read failure to stderr while skipping that entry, and install a SIGINT handler so that when Ctrl+C is pressed the I2C handle is closed, the driver library is terminated, and the program exits cleanly.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that continuously reads temperature and humidity from a Texas Instruments HDC2010 sensor on I2C bus 1 using the documented address, polling the sensor’s MEASUREMENT_CONFIG register until bit 0 clears or a timeout of roughly 500 ms occurs, then outputs the readings to the console every five seconds; the implementation must check the result of every driver call, detect a missing sensor (NAK) and any bus‑error conditions, retry transient I2C failures only up to a defined maximum count, and include a clean shutdown triggered by Ctrl +C via a signal handler that sets a volatile sig_atomic_t flag, closes the I2C handle, and invokes the library’s API call() before exiting.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that periodically reads the differential pressure from a Sensirion SDP800-500Pa on I2C bus 1 using the documented I2C address, waits approximately 45 ms for each measurement to complete, and logs to the console the raw 16‑bit pressure and temperature values every 500 ms; the program must open the I2C bus, verify that the driver library initializes correctly, check the result of every write and read operation, read exactly six bytes (two bytes pressure, one CRC, two bytes temperature, one CRC), validate each CRC‑8 checksum using the documented polynomial and initial value, handle sensor‑absent and bus‑error conditions gracefully, and on receipt of a SIGINT perform a clean shutdown by closing the I2C handle and invoking the library’s cleanup API on all exit paths.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that implements a PID‑controlled reflow oven using a MAX6675 thermocouple amplifier and a solid‑state relay, communicating with the MAX6675 over SPI0 (using either CE0 or CE1 as appropriate) and driving the solid‑state relay from GPIO17 (BCM numbering); the program must read the temperature from the thermocouple at a 1 Hz rate, update the SSR duty cycle based on the PID output (scaled 0.0 to 1.0) over a 1‑second period, log each temperature reading to a file named reflow_log.csv, load the target temperature profile from profile.txt where each line contains time_seconds,target_temp_celsius, apply robust error handling for all SPI communication and GPIO control including sensor‑absent and bus‑error conditions, and ensure that all resources are cleanly released on every exit path by handling termination signals.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that implements a PID‑controlled greenhouse heater using a DS18B20 temperature sensor and a 12 V heater driven through a relay and hardware PWM; the DS18B20 data line must be connected to GPIO4 (physical pin 7) on the 1‑wire bus accessed via the w1‑gpio kernel module at /sys/bus/w1/devices/, the relay enable line to GPIO17 (physical pin 11), and the PWM duty control to GPIO18 (physical pin 12) using the hardware PWM channel, while the program must accept command‑line arguments specifying the desired temperature setpoint and the PID gains Kp, Ki, and Kd, read the sensor periodically, validate the CRC of each DS18B20 reading and handle sensor‑absent or bus‑error conditions, compute the PID output, set the appropriate PWM duty cycle and relay state, and log every 5 seconds to a file named greenhouse.log a line containing the timestamp, average temperature, setpoint, PID output and PWM duty cycle; all I/O operations must be checked for errors, and the program must install SIGINT/SIGTERM handlers that on any exit path cleanly release resources by turning off the relay, setting PWM to zero, closing any opened file descriptors or device handles, and closing the log file.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that continuously reads humidity from an AHT20 sensor on the I2C bus /dev/i2c-1 using the documented address, triggering a measurement, waiting 80 ms, then reading the 6‑byte result while verifying that the status byte reports calibrated and not busy, retrying any failed I2C transaction up to three times with a 10 ms pause between attempts, and logging each humidity reading together with a timestamp to the console; the program must poll the sensor every 5 seconds, activate a dehumidifier relay connected to GPIO17 (active‑high) whenever the humidity exceeds 60 % and deactivate it when the humidity falls below 55 %, handle the case where the sensor is absent or all retries fail by printing an error message to stderr without terminating, and respond to SIGINT and SIGTERM by cleanly releasing the GPIO line, closing the I2C file descriptor and exiting with status 0.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that reads the relative humidity from an HTU21D sensor on the I2C bus /dev/i2c-1 using the documented I2C address, polls the sensor every 60 seconds, and posts the reading as a JSON document to http://api.example.com/humidity via an HTTP POST implemented with standard POSIX sockets; the program must employ syslog for all logging, include robust error handling for I2C communication failures such as NACKs, bus errors, CRC mismatches, or sensor absence as well as for any HTTP transmission errors, and must also catch SIGINT and SIGTERM to perform a graceful shutdown that cleanly closes all open file descriptors.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that continuously monitors a Bosch BMP280 pressure sensor on I2C‑1, using the documented I2C address, first verifying that the chip ID matches the documented value, then applying the Bosch compensation formulas to obtain pressure readings; the program must wait approximately 10 ms after each trigger for conversion completion, sample the sensor every 2 seconds, and record any pressure values that exceed 1020 hPa or fall below 980 hPa to a file named pressure_log.txt with timestamps, while handling I2C errors gracefully by attempting up to three retries that re‑open the bus and re‑verify the chip ID, and must include signal handlers for SIGINT and SIGTERM to ensure a clean shutdown that closes the I2C handle and invokes the library’s call() function on all exit paths.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4B that reads temperature from a TMP117, humidity from an AHT20, and motion detection from a PIR motion sensor, logging the values to daily timestamped CSV files with a header line “Timestamp,Temperature(C),Humidity(%),MotionDetected”; the TMP117 and AHT20 are connected on /dev/i2c-1, the PIR sensor is accessed via the library’s API call on line 17 and is wired to GPIO17 (gpiochip4 line 17, input), the program must sample every 1 second, retry I2C reads up to three times with a 10 ms backoff on failure, create a new log file at midnight each day, print a warning but continue if a sensor is not present at startup, handle I2C errors as described, and ensure all resources are cleanly released on every exit path including SIGINT and SIGTERM, building the code with gcc -o logger logger.c -lgpiod -lrt while using the documented I2C addresses for the TMP117 and AHT20.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that continuously monitors a YL‑83 rain sensor connected to GPIO17 (active‑low) via the GPIO bus, polling the sensor every 2 seconds, and when rain is detected commands an L298N motor driver to close a window by driving the motor forward for exactly 5 seconds using ENA on GPIO22, IN1 on GPIO23 and IN2 on GPIO24, then stops the motor; each detection, motor start, motor stop, and any error condition must be logged to stdout with a timestamp, the code must check the return status of every driver call and explicitly handle the situation where the GPIO chip cannot be opened, and it must install SIGINT and SIGTERM handlers so that on program termination the motor is safely stopped and all GPIO lines are released, while deliberately excluding any DHT22 or humidity sensing functionality.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that modulates a common‑anode RGB LED connected on the GPIO bus with the red cathode on GPIO17, the green cathode on GPIO22, and the blue cathode on GPIO27, sampling the system every 500 ms to read the CPU load from /proc/stat by comparing successive samples and mapping the 0‑100 % load to a color gradient where 0 % is green (0,255,0), 50 % is yellow (255,255,0) and 100 % is red (255,0,0), using hardware PWM via the driver library to set PWM values clamped to 0‑255 for each channel, handling driver library initialization failures by printing an error to stderr and exiting with code 1, and installing signal handlers for SIGINT and SIGTERM that turn the LED off (all channels full off for a common‑anode LED) and cleanly invoke the library’s API call() before exiting.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that reads temperature and pressure from a Bosch BMP280 sensor on I2C‑1 (SDA = GPIO2/pin 3, SCL = GPIO3/pin 5) using the documented I2C address, waits for each measurement to complete before reading, and every 5 seconds formats the two values into a JSON string and transmits it via UDP to 192.168.1.100 on port 5000; the program must handle all I2C read/write errors, sensor‑absent conditions, and UDP send failures gracefully, and must install SIGINT and SIGTERM handlers that cleanly release the I2C handle, close the UDP socket, and shut down the driver library on any exit path.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that dynamically controls a PWM‑driven cooling fan based on temperature readings from a MAX31855 thermocouple amplifier connected on SPI0 (CE0, GPIO8); the fan PWM must be output on GPIO18 (BCM) using hardware PWM at 1 kHz with a duty range of 0‑255, the program shall read the temperature every 1 second, compute the duty cycle using a piecewise fan curve (0 % below 25 °C, linear ramp from 0 % to 50 % between 25 °C and 40 °C, steeper ramp from 50 % to 200 % between 40 °C and 60 °C, and 100 % above 60 °C), store each timestamp, temperature, and PWM duty cycle in a 20‑entry circular buffer, perform robust error checking for every the driver library call (the library's API call, the library's API call, the library's API call, the library's API call); on any SPI transfer error or MAX31855 fault, print a diagnostic to stderr and skip the fan update for that cycle, initialize the driver library and open SPI channel 0 at 500 kHz mode 0, and on receipt of SIGINT stop the PWM, close the SPI interface, print the full contents of the circular buffer, terminate the driver library and then exit.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B running Bookworm or later that reads the RPM from a Melexis MLX90217 Hall‑effect sensor connected to the GPIO bus, with the sensor output wired to physical pin 7 (BCM GPIO4), by configuring the pin as an input with the internal pull‑up resistor enabled and counting rising‑edge pulses using GPIO interrupts; the program must count pulses in a one‑second window using an atomic add for the pulse counter, compute the revolutions per minute, and log one sample per second to a file named rpm_log.txt in the format “YYYY‑MM‑DD HH:MM:SS <rpm>” while also printing the same line to stdout, flushing the file after each write; it must check every driver‑library call and the file‑open call for errors, exiting with a diagnostic message on failure, but if the sensor is absent or not rotating it should log an RPM of 0 instead of aborting; finally, the program must install SIGINT and SIGTERM handlers that disable the timer and alert callback, close the log file, and invoke the library’s cleanup API call before exiting.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that uses two Melexis MLX90217 unipolar Hall‑effect sensors connected on the GPIO bus in an interrupt‑driven quadrature configuration, with Sensor A wired to GPIO17 (BCM) and Sensor B to GPIO27 (BCM) and hardware pull‑up resistors providing the required 90° electrical offset, to detect the direction of rotation and log each clockwise or counter‑clockwise event to a file named rotation_log.txt using millisecond‑precision timestamps formatted as “YYYY‑MM‑DD HH:MM:SS.mmm”; the implementation must employ the driver’s edge‑triggered alerts via the library’s API call for interrupt handling (without using any other driver library), maintain a quadrature state machine that tracks the previous state to infer direction, protect the shared state between the ISR and the main thread with a mutex, have the main loop wait on a condition variable or sleep rather than busy‑wait, check all error paths including each of the three library’s API call() invocations and the file open operation, and install a signal handler for SIGINT and SIGTERM that performs a graceful shutdown by flushing and closing the log file and terminating the driver library.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that uses the GPIO bus to monitor a SainSmart TTP223B digital capacitive touch sensor connected to GPIO23 (physical pin 16, BCM 23) and to drive an LED on GPIO18 (physical pin 12, BCM 18) with an appropriate current‑limiting resistor, polling the sensor every 50 ms so that the LED is illuminated only while the sensor is actively touched; the program must open the GPIO chip, request the input line for the sensor and the output line for the LED, check the return status of every driver call including chip opening, line requests, reads and writes, handle the situation where the GPIO chip is unavailable, log startup, shutdown, each touch event and any errors to the system syslog using openlog/syslog, and install SIGINT and SIGTERM handlers that perform a graceful shutdown by turning the LED off and releasing all resources before exiting.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that reads touch input from a SainSmart TTP223B capacitive touch sensor connected on the GPIO bus, using the sensor’s OUT line on GPIO17 (physical pin 11) to capture rising‑edge events and toggles an LED attached to GPIO18 (physical pin 12) on each detected touch; the program must employ the line event interface to wait for rising edges rather than polling, apply a software debounce of approximately 50 ms after each rising‑edge detection, initialize the LED line as an output and drive it LOW at startup, verify the result of every driver call (chip open, line request, event wait, read, write) and print clear error messages to stderr when a call fails, and handle SIGINT and SIGTERM by gracefully releasing all driver resources (lines and chip) before exiting.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that continuously monitors a Raindrop Sensor Module with a digital output connected to GPIO17 (BCM) on the GPIO bus, enabling the internal pull‑up resistor on that pin so the input is defined when the sensor is disconnected, and polls the pin every 500 ms; the program must detect the active‑low condition where a LOW (0) level indicates rain and a HIGH (1) level indicates no rain, and it should write timestamped “Rain Detected” or “No Rain” messages to /var/log/rain_events.log only when the state changes, while checking the return value of every driver library call and of fopen, and it must handle SIGINT and SIGTERM to perform a graceful shutdown that closes the log file and releases any driver resources on all exit paths.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that reads ambient light data from a Texas Instruments OPT3001 sensor connected on I2C bus 1 (/dev/i2c-1) for a smart greenhouse environment monitoring system, performing a read once per second while waiting at least 100 ms after writing the configuration before reading the result, formatting each measurement as “YYYY‑MM‑DD HH:MM:SS, <lux_value>” with two decimal places into a file named light_data.txt and also printing it to stdout, rigorously checking the return value of every driver library call and every file I/O operation and printing a descriptive error to stderr and skipping that iteration if any call fails (exiting gracefully on initialization failure), installing a SIGINT handler that on clean shutdown closes the I2C handle, calls the appropriate library cleanup function, and ensures the log file is flushed and closed on all exit paths, and handling the fact that the driver library uses little‑endian word order while the OPT3001 provides data in big‑endian format by byte‑swapping the 16‑bit values before writing them to the sensor and after reading them back.

prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the GPIO bus with BCM numbering to control a KY‑019 relay module connected to GPIO 18, listening on TCP port 5000 for case‑insensitive commands “ON” and “OFF” (trailing whitespace must be ignored), invoking the library’s API call to switch the relay and logging every activation, deactivation, and any invalid‑command event with a timestamp to a file named relay_log.txt; the implementation must include comprehensive error handling for all socket operations (creation, bind, listen, accept, and read) as well as for GPIO initialization, and must install SIGINT and SIGTERM handlers that gracefully shut down the library’s API call, close the sockets and the log file, turn off the relay, and terminate the driver library.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that continuously monitors two Sensirion SLF3S‑1300F liquid‑flow sensors (40 ml/min version) connected to I2C bus 1, using the documented I2C addresses for sensor 1 and sensor 2, and controls a safety relay on GPIO 18 (BCM numbering, active‑high) with a 100 ms polling loop; each iteration must read three bytes from each sensor, validate the CRC‑8 using the documented polynomial, initial value and no final XOR, and if a read returns fewer than three bytes or the CRC check fails, a warning is written to stderr and the cycle is skipped without changing the relay state, otherwise the flow rates are logged with millisecond timestamps to flow_log.txt in append mode with an immediate flush, and if both reads succeed and either sensor reports a flow below 5.0 ml/min the relay is energized (write 1) and otherwise de‑energized (write 0) when both are at or above 5.0 ml/min; the program must check the library’s API return codes for opening I2C bus 1 with flags 0 for each sensor, verify that the start‑measurement command write (the documented two‑byte sequence) returns 0 for each sensor, and also verify the GPIO 18 configuration call’s return code, performing full cleanup of any partially‑initialized resources on any failure, and on shutdown triggered by SIGINT or SIGTERM it must de‑energize the relay, close any open I2C handles, call the library’s cleanup function, and print a shutdown message, while compiling cleanly with gcc ‑Wall ‑Wextra.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that continuously monitors the Seeed Studio Rain Sensor v1.0 digital output on GPIO 17 (BCM) configured as an input with a pull‑up, polling every 200 ms over the GPIO bus, and drives a DC motor window actuator through an L298N driver using ENA on GPIO 22 (BCM), IN1 on GPIO 23 (BCM) and IN2 on GPIO 24 (BCM); the sensor pulls its DO pin low when rain is present and high when dry, so the program must detect a rising‑edge (dry‑to‑wet transition) and, on that edge only, start the close‑window sequence by setting ENA high, IN1 high, IN2 low, holding the motor for exactly 5 seconds using the library’s API call() or usleep() (no busy‑wait), then stopping the motor by setting ENA low and both IN1 and IN2 low while verifying each call, logging all events with syslog (facility LOG_USER, identifier “rain_window”) as LOG_INFO for startup, rain detection, motor start/stop and shutdown and using LOG_ERR or LOG_WARNING for any call failures, suppressing further triggers until the sensor reads dry for at least three consecutive polls (≈600 ms), and handling SIGINT and SIGTERM to perform a graceful shutdown that stops the motor (all calls LOW), calls the library’s API call() to clean up, closes syslog and exits cleanly, with every library API call return checked and logged, all within a single‑process design without forks.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi that uses the GPIO bus to control a hobby servo acting as a door‑lock actuator based on two momentary push‑buttons, with the servo connected to GPIO 18 (physical pin 12, BCM 18), the lock button to GPIO 21 (BCM) and the unlock button to GPIO 22 (BCM), both buttons wired to ground when pressed and therefore requiring internal pull‑up resistors to be enabled; the program must poll the buttons in a tight loop with a small sleep to keep CPU usage low, implement debouncing by waiting for the button release plus a short delay so that a single press is not registered multiple times, drive the library’s API call() with a 2000 µs pulse width when the GPIO 21 button is pressed to lock, a 1000 µs pulse width when the GPIO 22 button is pressed to unlock, and output status messages to stdout for lock, unlock, and shutdown events, verify that the API call() returns success for both pulse‑width commands and exit with an error message on failure, and install a SIGINT/SIGTERM handler that stops the servo by sending a pulse width of 0, calls the API call() one final time, and then exits.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that monitors a PIR motion sensor on GPIO 4 (physical pin 7, BCM 4) using a 100 ms polling interval and, on each rising edge, activates a relay‑controlled 12 V LED floodlight connected to GPIO 17 (physical pin 11, BCM 17) for exactly 60 seconds before turning it off, while appending activation events with an ISO‑8601 timestamp and deactivation events with a timestamp and the measured duration in seconds to a file named security_log.txt; the program must verify that the driver library is successfully initialized, check the return code of every library API call as well as the result of every fopen, fprintf and fclose operation, and if any file operation fails it must turn off the floodlight before exiting, and it must install a SIGINT/SIGTERM handler that cleanly turns off the floodlight, releases the driver library resources, and exits with code 0, ensuring that the floodlight is OFF on all exit paths and that no driver library is used directly in the code.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that uses the MPR121 capacitive touch sensor on I2C bus 1 (using the documented address) to toggle a relay connected to GPIO17 (BCM) only on a fresh rising‑edge touch of electrode 0, applying a 200 ms debounce to that electrode, performing a full MPR121 initialization that includes a soft‑reset, configuration of baseline filtering (MHD, NHD, NCL, FDL) to the documented values, setting the debounce to the documented value, configuring FFI, SFI and CDT to the documented values, enabling auto‑config with the documented range, and enabling exactly 12 electrodes as documented; the program must set the relay to a known OFF state at startup and also ensure it is OFF on shutdown, must implement robust error handling for every driver library and I2C call by checking return values and handling sensor‑absent and bus‑error conditions, and must cleanly release all resources on every exit path, including handling SIGINT and SIGTERM.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that uses the GPIO bus to control a servo motor on BCM GPIO17 and read a PIR sensor on BCM GPIO4, listening for TCP connections on port 5000; the program must accept commands of the form “the library's API call <angle>” where <angle> is 0‑180 and generate a software PWM signal at 50 Hz with a 1‑2 ms pulse width to position the servo, and also respond to the command “PIR” by sending back “PIR:0” or “PIR:1” over the socket, while logging all events, commands, and errors to both syslog (LOG_USER facility) and a file named security.log with ISO 8601 timestamps, checking the result of every driver library call, socket syscall, and file I/O operation and, if GPIO initialization fails, logging the error and exiting with a non‑zero status; the code must include <stdarg.h> for variadic functions so it compiles cleanly with -Wall -Wextra, and it must handle SIGINT and SIGTERM to perform a graceful shutdown that releases all driver resources, closes the socket and the log file.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that generates a haptic feedback system by pulsing two Precision Microdrives 310‑101 vibration motors sequentially and repeatedly over the GPIO bus, driving motor 1 through a driver circuit attached to GPIO17 (BCM) for 200 ms, then motor 2 through a driver circuit attached to GPIO27 (BCM) for 300 ms, and looping this pattern indefinitely; the design must include robust error handling that checks every driver library call for line request failures and value write failures, as well as proper registration of signal handlers, and must handle SIGINT and SIGTERM to gracefully release the GPIO lines and stop the motors by invoking the library’s API call() on all exit paths, while observing the constraint that the motors require 3 V at 60 mA typical and therefore must be driven through an external driver circuit such as an NPN transistor with a flyback diode rather than being connected directly to the GPIO pins.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that implements a sound‑triggered alarm as a single executable with two selectable modes chosen by a command‑line argument; in the sound_sensor mode the program polls the LM393 sound sensor on its digital output pin connected to GPIO17 (BCM) every 10 ms, treats a logic 0 on this active‑low pin as a sound event, and publishes an alert on a ZeroMQ socket bound to tcp://*:5555 using the topic SOUND_ALERTS, while in the alarm_node mode the program subscribes to tcp://localhost:5555 for the same topic and, upon receiving a message, lights an alarm LED attached to GPIO27 (BCM) for exactly 1 second; the implementation must use the GPIO bus directly without any driver library, provide robust error handling for every GPIO and ZeroMQ call, and install handlers for SIGINT and SIGTERM that perform a clean shutdown by releasing the GPIO lines, the GPIO chip, and all ZeroMQ sockets and context on every exit path.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that uses an IR receiver such as the TSOP38238 connected to GPIO17 (BCM) to decode NEC infrared remote signals and report the decoded commands both to syslog and to an MQTT broker at localhost on port 1883 using the topic ir/decoded, publishing the command as a JSON object; the program must register an alert callback on the falling edge of the GPIO to capture pulse timings, interpret the NEC frame consisting of a 9 ms mark followed by a 4.5 ms space header, 560 µs marks for each bit, a 1690 µs space for logic‑1 and a 560 µs space for logic‑0, decode the full 32‑bit frame, validate the command against its inverted copy while allowing extended NEC frames that omit inverted‑address validation, check driver initialization and GPIO setup failures, guard against pulse‑buffer overflow, verify the NEC checksum, initialize the MQTT client once at startup and invoke the network loop in the main loop, and ensure clean release of all resources—including the driver, MQTT client, and syslog—when the process receives SIGINT or SIGTERM.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that reads ambient light from four BH1750FVI sensors attached to I2C‑1, waiting 180 ms after each start‑conversion command, and repeats this acquisition loop once per second; for each sensor the program must issue an ioctl(I2C_SLAVE, addr) before any transaction, may use a single /dev/i2c-1 descriptor or one per sensor, and must not rely on any external driver library, handling any open, address‑set, write, read or partial‑read failure by inserting a NaN value for that sensor while continuing with the others; after gathering the lux values it must broadcast a UDP multicast packet to 239.255.255.250:5005 containing a semicolon‑separated list of sensor_id,lux pairs such as 1,120.5;2,85.0;3,210.5;4,45.0, and it must install handlers for SIGINT and SIGTERM that set a termination flag so the loop can exit cleanly, ensuring that all file descriptors for I2C and the UDP socket are closed on every exit path.
